hints: Look at what R is pointing to - two identical vertical rods joined together at the middle. What do you call the two copies made when DNA replicates?
Now look at S - the oval joining the two rods in the middle where spindle fibres will attach. What is this constricted region called?
walkthrough:
See What R Is Pointing To**
After DNA replication each chromosome consists of two identical DNA copies held together. These two identical copies are sister chromatids. In Fig. 7.1, R points to the two rods of the left-hand chromosome, so R is sister chromatids.

See What S Is Holding Together**
The two sister chromatids are held together at a constricted region in the middle. This is the centromere, the site where spindle microtubules attach in cell division. S labels this oval region on both chromosomes.
Final answer: R - (sister) chromatids; S - centromere.

hints: Compare the letters down the left chromosome (G to M) with those down the right chromosome (g to m). What does this tell you about the genes they carry?
Look at the order and position of each letter and the position of the oval S. What is the same about where each gene sits?
Now compare overall size and shape - length and centromere position - and remember what homologous chromosomes do in prophase 1.
walkthrough:
Same Genes In The Same Order**
Homologous means the same in structure but not necessarily the same in alleles. Both chromosomes carry the seven genes G/g to M/m in the same order down the chromosome. One carries all dominant alleles, the other all recessive alleles.

Same Loci And Same Centromere Position**
A locus is the fixed position of a gene on a chromosome. G and g are at the same locus, H and h at the same locus, and so on. The centromere S is also at the same position on both - roughly in the middle - so the arm lengths match.

Same Length To Form A Pair**
The two chromosomes are the same length and pair up together in meiosis to form a bivalent. That pairing behaviour visible in Fig. 7.1 is itself evidence they are homologues.
Final answer: Any three from: carry same genes; genes at same loci / position; same position of centromere S; same length / size; pair to form a bivalent.

hints: In Fig. 7.2 point T is between I/i and J/j on the two inner chromatids only. Which alleles are above the break and which stay below?
If those top pieces swap over, think about what each of the four chromatids will now carry at the top versus the bottom.
walkthrough:
Only The Inner Chromatids Exchange**
Crossing over is the exchange of segments between non-sister chromatids. At T, the break is between I and J. So the segment G-H-I on the inner left chromatid swaps with the segment g-h-i on the inner right chromatid. The parts below T, J-K-L-M and j-k-l-m, do not move.

Build The Four New Chromatids**
Left chromosome: outer chromatid stays G H I J K L M, inner chromatid becomes g h i on top joined to J K L M below. Right chromosome: inner chromatid becomes G H I on top joined to j k l m below, outer chromatid stays g h i j k l m. That is why the top three letters are now different on each pair, while all the lower letters are the same on each pair.

Final answer: Left chromosome: one chromatid G H I J K L M (unchanged) and one chromatid g h i J K L M (recombinant); Right chromosome: one chromatid G H I j k l m (recombinant) and one chromatid g h i j k l m (unchanged). So top three alleles differ within each pair, lower alleles are identical within each pair.

hints: Crossing over needs homologous chromosomes to be closely paired as bivalents - in which first-division stage does this pairing happen?
walkthrough:
When Homologues Are Paired**
Homologous chromosomes come together to form bivalents and swap segments only in prophase I of meiosis, before they are separated in anaphase I. So crossing over occurs in prophase I.

hints: Picture all the different bivalents lined up in the middle of the cell in metaphase I. Is there a fixed rule about which side the maternal and paternal chromosome faces?
Think about what happens when the homologues are then pulled apart - how does that random facing affect which chromosomes go together into the same daughter cell?
Link that different chromosome mix to alleles - why does a new mix of whole chromosomes mean a new mix of alleles?
walkthrough:
Random Orientation On The Equator**
In metaphase I each bivalent lines up on the equator / metaphase plate. Which way round it lines up is random and independent of all the other bivalents. For one pair the maternal chromosome may face left and paternal face right, while for the next pair it is the opposite.

Random Separation Gives New Chromosome Mixes**
When homologues are pulled apart in anaphase I, that random orientation decides which daughter cell gets the maternal chromosome and which gets the paternal chromosome for each pair. With many pairs this produces many different combinations of whole maternal and paternal chromosomes in the gametes.

New Chromosome Mix Means New Allele Mix**
Because maternal and paternal chromosomes carry different alleles, each new combination of chromosomes is a new combination of alleles. This is independent assortment, giving for example $2^{n}$ possible combinations, $2^{23}$ in humans, and so greatly increases genetic variation.

Final answer: Any three from: homologous chromosomes / bivalents align independently at the equator / metaphase plate in metaphase I; maternal and paternal homologues orient randomly; this gives different combinations of chromosomes in daughter cells; giving new combinations of alleles, e.g. $2^{n}$ combinations, $2^{23}$ in humans.
